prompt: In a trace view, why does the longest bar rarely answer where the time went?
hint: What does a parent do while its children run?

choices.text: Because the longest bar is usually an internal span, which nobody instruments
choices.why: The longest is usually the root, a server span.

choices.text: Because it is usually the root, which lasts as long as the children it waits for
Because Jaeger draws bars on a logarithmic scale
Because a span's duration is only an estimate made by the store

prompt: What is a span's self time?
hint: The part that belongs to nobody below.

choices.text: The time between the span's start and its first child's start
The span's duration as measured by the store rather than by the service
choices.why: Same duration, different clock; not self time.

choices.text: Its duration minus the time spent inside its children
The time its service spent on the CPU
choices.why: Self time includes waiting on anything uninstrumented.

prompt: `POST /orders` shows 25 ms of self time that no child accounts for. What is the most likely explanation?

choices.text: Work nobody instrumented: publishing to RabbitMQ over a new connection
choices.why: Right: self time is where uninstrumented work shows up.

choices.text: The clock difference between the orders container and the payments container
The time the mailer spent sending the confirmation e-mail
choices.why: That ran after the parent ended and is not subtracted.

choices.text: Jaeger rounding every child down to the nearest millisecond
choices.why: Rounding is under a millisecond per span.

prompt: A child span starts after its parent has ended. How much should it reduce the parent's self time?

choices.text: Its whole duration
choices.why: The parent was not waiting for it.

choices.text: Half its duration
choices.why: There is no overlap to split.

choices.text: Nothing
choices.why: Right: none of it falls inside the parent.

choices.text: Its duration plus the gap before it
choices.why: That would make self time negative.

prompt: Put the steps of reading a slow trace in order.
hint: Find the work, then ask about it.
items: Find the trace, by an id from a log or by a search
Pick the span with the most self time on the critical path
Read that span's attributes and its log lines

prompt: A handler calls prices (280 ms) and stock (120 ms) at the same time. Stock is made twice as fast. What happens to the request?
hint: Which call does the request wait for?

choices.text: It becomes 60 ms faster
choices.why: Stock was not what it waited for.

choices.text: It takes as long as before
It becomes half as long
It becomes slower, because stock now finishes before prices does and has to wait

prompt: In the parallel example, prices takes 280 ms and stock 120 ms. How many milliseconds of slack does stock have?
How do you find the critical path of a request in its trace?

choices.text: Follow the spans with the most self time from the root down
choices.why: Self time can sit off the critical path.

choices.text: Follow the first child of every span
choices.why: The first to start is not the last to finish.

choices.text: From the root's end, step into the child that finished last, and repeat
Pick the spans marked as errors
choices.why: Errors and the critical path are different questions.

prompt: Two calls are made parallel to save time. What should you read next in the new traces?

choices.text: Nothing: a parallel request has no critical path
The sibling that is now slowest, which the critical path runs through
The faster sibling, since parallel calls compete for the CPU and it now takes longer
choices.why: The slower one ends the request.

choices.text: The root, whose self time is now all of the request
choices.why: The root still waits for its children.

prompt: Is the mailer on the critical path of the checkout?
hint: Did the customer wait for it?

choices.text: Yes, every span in the trace is on it
No, but it is on the path of when the e-mail arrives
Only while the queue is empty
choices.why: The checkout never waits for the mailer.

choices.text: Yes, whenever the mailer happens to be the slowest service in the trace
choices.why: Speed does not put it on the path.

prompt: A search in Jaeger for slow checkouts returns nothing for an hour you know was slow. Which explanation fits the section?

choices.text: The search form only accepts the last fifteen minutes
choices.why: The window is yours to choose.

choices.text: Slow traces are never exported, by design
choices.why: Nothing filters on duration by default.

choices.text: The traces were not kept: sampled out, expired, or lost on a restart
Jaeger searches by trace id only
choices.why: It searches by service, operation, duration and tags.

prompt: Why could you search the shop's checkouts by product?

choices.text: Jaeger reads the request body of every span
choices.why: It sees only what the span carries.

choices.text: The storefront writes `shop.sku` on its span
Automatic instrumentation adds the product to every span
The Collector copies it from the logs
choices.why: The span carries it from the start.

prompt: Which of these can a Jaeger search filter on? Choose all that apply.

choices.text: The service
The operation name
A minimum duration
The customer's IP address, when no span carries it
A line of the service's source code

prompt: The lab exports every span to both Jaeger and Zipkin. Where is that choice made?

choices.text: In each service's SDK, with two exporters
In Jaeger, which forwards a copy to Zipkin
In the Collector's configuration
In Grafana's data sources

prompt: Match each span kind to the side it records.
Zipkin's dependency graph shows storefront → orders → payments, but no mailer. Why?

choices.text: The mailer's spans are in a different trace from the checkout's
choices.why: They are in the same trace.

choices.text: Zipkin drops spans that start more than a second after the root
No producer span and no broker named, so the queue makes no edge
The mailer was stopped during the window
choices.why: It ran for most of it.

prompt: A dependency graph built from traces lacks an edge you expected. What does that tell you first?
hint: The map draws what is recorded.

choices.text: That the two services never talk to each other
That the instrumentation may not record that call
That the store may have run out of memory
choices.why: A whole edge, not random spans.

choices.text: That the graph needs a longer lookback to be drawn at all

prompt: The checkout's trace lists as 26 seconds long, yet the customer waited 0.44 s. Which number describes the customer?
hint: Which span did they wait for?

choices.text: The root span's duration
The trace's length, from first start to last end
The mailer's span
choices.why: The customer never waited for it.

choices.text: The sum of every span's duration
choices.why: Nested spans would be counted twice.

prompt: During the mailer's stop, why did the oldest messages wait longest?

choices.text: RabbitMQ delivers the newest messages first
choices.why: A queue is first in, first out.

choices.text: All were taken in one burst at restart, oldest first
choices.why: Right: the oldest had been there longest.

choices.text: The oldest messages were larger
The mailer retries old messages three times before it takes the new ones

prompt: Between two real hosts, a queue wait computed from two spans comes out as −3 ms. What is it?

choices.text: A message delivered before it was published
Clock skew between the hosts, noise around a short wait
A bug in the propagation of the context between the two services
A message that skipped the queue entirely

prompt: A trace store measures a trace from its first span's start to its last span's ___.
A failed checkout has four red spans. Which one is the origin?

choices.text: The root, because the customer saw the error there
choices.why: It reports what came from below.

choices.text: The first one in the list Zipkin returns
choices.why: The list's order is not depth.

choices.text: The deepest red span with no red child
The one with the longest duration

prompt: A service catches an exception and answers 200. What does its trace show?
hint: A red span is marked by somebody.

choices.text: No error anywhere, unless the code sets the status itself
A red span, since the SDK records every exception
choices.why: Only one that escapes the span.

choices.text: An error on the caller's span only
A gap in the trace where the span should be

prompt: The deepest red span is payments, naming a card network that nobody instruments. What does that mean for the diagnosis?
hint: The deepest place you can see.

choices.text: The fault is certainly in the payments code
choices.why: It may be one step beyond.

choices.text: The fault may lie beyond what the traces can see
The trace may be broken and should be discarded
choices.why: It is accurate up to its edge.

choices.text: The orders span is the real origin

prompt: What is an exemplar?

choices.text: A histogram bucket that has been sampled
choices.why: It is a trace id, not a bucket.

choices.text: The trace id of one real request, kept beside a bucket's count
A typical log line attached to a dashboard
The example value an alert keeps beside its rule, showing what made it fire
choices.why: That is not what the word means here.

prompt: Which pieces had to agree for exemplars to reach Prometheus? Choose all that apply.

choices.text: The code observes with the current trace id
The scrape asks for and gets OpenMetrics
Prometheus runs with exemplar storage enabled
Jaeger is configured to push ids to Prometheus
Loki indexes the trace id

prompt: Why does the storefront expose no exemplars while orders does?

choices.text: The storefront is not scraped by Prometheus
The storefront's spans are sampled out
Its span has ended by the time the duration is observed
The storefront answers only in the classic text format

prompt: A scrape receives the classic text format instead of OpenMetrics. What happens to exemplars?

choices.text: They arrive in a separate file
They are not sent at all
They arrive as extra labels on each bucket
They arrive but Grafana cannot draw them

prompt: A latency graph shows a slow bucket filling up. Put the steps from that graph to a cause in order.
hint: Each step uses one join of the lesson.
items: Click an exemplar dot in the slow bucket
Open the trace it names in Jaeger
Find the span on the critical path with the most self time
Read that span's attributes and the log lines with its trace id

prompt: Match each question to the place in this lesson that answers it.

pairs.left: Which services call which, and how often?
Which checkouts took over 400 ms in the last hour?
Which request is behind this point on the graph?
How long did the confirmations sit in RabbitMQ?
pairs.right: the gap between two spans across the queue

prompt: A trace reads: root 900 ms, self 5; `GET /price` 850 ms, self 840; `GET /stock` 300 ms, self 300, run in parallel with `GET /price`. Which change shortens the request most?
hint: Which span is on the critical path, and whose time is its own?

choices.text: Making `GET /stock` twice as fast, because it is the second biggest
choices.why: It has slack; the request does not wait for it.

choices.text: Making the work inside `GET /price` faster
choices.why: Right: on the critical path, and its own.

choices.text: Removing the root's five milliseconds of self time
Running `GET /stock` before `GET /price` instead of beside it
choices.why: That adds 300 ms to the path.
